# A voice in the room — plan and research

Plan and notes for the AI article on local voice agents: what "speech to
speech" means when nothing leaves the house, the three shapes every local
voice agent takes, the three projects the question named — Voicebox, VoxCPM,
Dograh — placed among the rest of the 2026 field, and the parts of a
household voice stack run and timed on a machine with no GPU. Started
2026-09-13. It follows "An Agent on Your Own Machine" — the same promise,
said out loud.

Audience: someone who has a local model running already, or is about to,
and wants to talk to it instead of typing — and wants to know which of the
dozens of projects with "voice" in the name is a model, which is a
framework, which is an app, and what each one needs.

## What was verified, and how

| Claim | Checked against |
|---|---|
| Versions, dates, Python requirements and licence fields of two dozen packages | PyPI's JSON API, queried from this machine — [`notes/voice-models.md`](/ai/research/voice-agents/voice-models.md) |
| What each project is, in its own words — architecture, sizes, languages, hardware line, latency claims, licence | The projects' GitHub READMEs and licence files, read in full (raw default branch); Dograh's `docker-compose.yaml` |
| That a household cascade runs on a CPU, and how fast | Kokoro, Silero VAD, three sherpa-onnx recognisers and openWakeWord installed and timed here on four cores — [`notes/voice-run.md`](/ai/research/voice-agents/voice-run.md), script [`notes/pipeline.py`](https://github.com/Collegica/collegica-code/blob/main/docs/research/2026-09-13-voice-agents/notes/pipeline.py) |
| Kyutai's serving figures, Voxtral Realtime, Qwen3.5-Omni, the Home Assistant Voice PE hardware and price, Sesame's unreleased 8B, the closed baselines' prices | Search-result snippets of the vendors' pages plus trade press — `huggingface.co`, `arxiv.org`, `kyutai.org`, `home-assistant.io`, `dograh.com`, `voicebox.sh`, the Pipecat and LiveKit docs sites and every vendor site were blocked by this session's egress policy. Marked *(search)* in the notes; lower confidence |

Not verified: any model hosted only on Hugging Face. VoxCPM2, Pocket TTS,
Moshi, Qwen3-TTS, Chatterbox, Smart Turn and the LiveKit turn detector
could not be downloaded, so their speeds are the projects' claims. Nothing
with an LLM in the loop was run either — the run measures the ears, the
mouth and the doorbell, not the brain. The article says so.

## Decisions

1. **Three shapes before thirty names.** Cascade (STT → LLM → TTS),
   speech-native half-duplex, full-duplex. The shape decides the hardware,
   the latency and the licence questions; the names slot in afterwards.
2. **The three names in the question are three different kinds of
   thing** — an app (Voicebox), a model (VoxCPM2), an orchestration
   platform (Dograh) — and the article says so early, because that is the
   most useful fact about them.
3. **Write from the reader's machine.** No GPU, maybe a Mac, maybe a
   Raspberry Pi. So the household cascade — the only shape that runs on a
   CPU — is the one measured, and the GPU shapes are described with their
   stated floors.
4. **Quote the projects, measure the parts.** Every latency in the article
   is labelled as a claim or as this machine's number.
5. **Licences get a table.** Two non-commercial surprises in an otherwise
   permissive field (openWakeWord's models, Fish Audio) and one GPL (Piper)
   are the kind of thing a reader finds out too late.
6. **Date everything.** Pipecat released the day before; Pocket TTS ten
   days before. The article names the day.
7. **No hero yet.** Generated (`hero.md`); the CDN was blocked; the article
   ships without a banner until the file is added — same as the robotics
   ones.

## Additions

- **2026-09-14 — VoiceStudio.** Added at a reader's suggestion as the
  fourth "name": a second local voice studio of the same shape as
  Voicebox, with sixteen TTS and eleven ASR engines, an OpenAI-compatible
  audio API and an MCP server, under AGPL-3.0 with non-commercial default
  weights. README and `LICENSE` read in full; repository metadata from
  GitHub's search API; the docs site was not fetched. A paragraph beside
  Voicebox, a TL;DR clause, a licence-table row, a "what to do" line and a
  source entry.

## Traps hit

- The first Kokoro download was a truncated file (194 of 325 MB) — a chained
  `curl … && …` was killed part-way and the later step skipped the file
  because it existed. ONNX Runtime reports it as "Protobuf parsing failed",
  which reads like a version problem. Check `Content-Length` against the
  file before blaming the runtime.
- `curl` against `github.com` HTML pages returns 403 through this proxy;
  release assets and raw files download fine. Read pages one way, fetch
  bytes another.
- Hugging Face is unreachable from here, which removes most of the field
  from any run: the sherpa-onnx project mirrors its models as GitHub
  release assets, and that is the only reason three recognisers could be
  timed.
- `pipecat-ai` has 52 optional extras and the local ones are not the
  defaults; `pip install pipecat-ai` alone gives a framework with nothing
  to hear or say.
- Dograh's Compose file has no speech or LLM container. "Runs on prem" is
  true of the platform, not of the models, unless you point it at your own
  servers.
- Licences hide in the weights: openWakeWord's code is Apache-2.0 and its
  pre-trained wake words CC-BY-NC-SA; Piper moved to GPL; Fish Audio S2
  Pro is research-only; PersonaPlex's weights carry NVIDIA's model licence
  on top of Moshi's CC-BY.
